svg.title: Module 04 one-page guide: When Not to Build an Agent
svg.text: CSCI 391 · MODULE 04 · ONE-PAGE LECTURE GUIDE
When Not to Build an Agent
Agents are a Swiss Army knife. Sometimes you only need the screwdriver.
Part I · Foundations and Mindset · Week 4 · Read: Caldwell, The Agentic AI Bible, Ch. 4
OPENING CASE
A team needs to route support emails into one of four queues. The agent prototype demos beautifully. A prompted
classifier with structured output does the same job for a fraction of the cost, with an accuracy ceiling you can read
straight off a confusion matrix.
If the answer to all four questions isn't clearly yes, stop and look for a
simpler system first.
KEY FRAMEWORK
The four-question decision rule
Is the trajectory open-ended?
Do the inputs vary in structure in ways a schema
can't capture?
Is the output space itself open?
Is there genuine action in the world, interleaved
with observation?
YOU SHOULD BE ABLE TO
Apply the four-question rule before starting agent
development
Choose among function calls, classifiers,
extraction, workflows, and agents
Compare build-cost vs. run-cost for classifier
options
Evaluate a classifier with a confusion matrix
ENTERPRISE LENS · ADDISON BOYER
When a stakeholder asks for 'an agent', I ask for ten real inputs and the ideal outputs. Half the time the outputs
have a fixed shape — that's a function call.
Shadow-run the simpler system next to the agent on real traffic and review the disagreements by hand before
deciding.
Rule of thumb: if violating a constraint would cause a production incident, it belongs in a re-injected constraint
or in code — not buried in a long prompt.
DISCUSS
→ How would you prove a problem needs adaptive action rather than a workflow?
→ What is the cheapest system that would meet the requirement?
Concepts after Caldwell, The Agentic AI Bible, Ch. 4. Case framing, synthesis, and enterprise lens: Addison Boyer.
